draft.title: Trade routes across the world
card: The Silk Road was a network of land routes across Asia. Traders often passed goods along it in stages, with few travelling the whole way.
Sea routes across the Indian Ocean and the seas around Asia also linked China, India, the Islamic world and Europe.
Traders carried goods such as silk and spices. They also carried ideas, such as new religions and new ways of making things.
Disease travelled with traders too. The Black Death, which killed millions of people in Europe in the 1300s, is thought to have spread along trade routes.
draft.remember: Trade routes moved goods, ideas and disease between distant places.

a.q: Why did the Silk Road matter for more than the goods sold along it?
opts: It also spread ideas and disease between regions
It let one empire rule all of the lands it crossed
It replaced sea routes as the way to trade with Asia
It was used only by traders who carried silk
a.why: Traders travelling the routes carried ideas and disease as well as goods, so the routes linked the lives of people far apart. The Silk Road did not replace sea routes, because the card says both linked the same regions.
a.clue: Think about what else travelled with the traders.

b.q: Tariq, a trader, sells spices in a city on the Silk Road. He hears about a new method of making paper from a trader who came from far away. What does this show about trade routes?
opts: Traders passed on ideas as well as goods
Traders only exchanged goods and never ideas
Trade routes were used only for spices and silk
Trade routes spread ideas but not goods
b.why: Tariq learns of a new way of making something from a passing trader, so ideas moved along the route. The wrong options say the routes carried only goods, or only ideas, but the card says they carried both.
b.clue: What did Tariq gain besides things to sell?

a.best: It also spread ideas and disease between regions

b.best: Traders passed on ideas as well as goods

problems.detail: Every wrong option uses an absolute ('only', 'never', 'but not'), and the right option is the only one without one. A student could pick it from wording alone. Two distractors ('used only for spices and silk' and 'only exchanged goods and never ideas') also say nearly the same thing.
